source_refs.note: Book p. 260-261: heading printed 14.1.2 (no 14.1.1); three perpendicular axes, drawing convention, right-hand rule, point P(a, b, c); 3 figures. Book error: 'curled images toward'. Teaching notes, Key points, Common mistakes are ours.

blocks.title: Numbering note
blocks.text: The textbook prints this heading as 14.1.2 (Book# 14.1.2). The book has no 14.1.1, so the portal numbers the sub-headings of 14.1 in sequence as 14.1.1 to 14.1.8; 14.1.1 here is the book's 14.1.2.

In space a rectangular coordinate system is constructed using three mutually orthogonal (perpendicular) axes, which have origin as their common point of intersection. When sketching figures, we follow the convention that the positive x-axis points towards the reader, the positive y-axis to the right and the positive z-axis points upwards.

blocks.alt: Three perpendicular axes through the origin O: the z-axis points up, the y-axis points to the right and the x-axis slants down to the left, toward the reader. The negative halves x′, y′ and z′ are dashed.
blocks.caption: Rectangular coordinate system in space: x toward the reader, y to the right, z upwards (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Think of a corner of your classroom floor. The two edges along the floor are the x- and y-axes, and the vertical edge where the walls meet is the z-axis; the corner itself is the origin \(O\). Each axis has a positive half (solid) and a negative half (dashed \(x'\), \(y'\), \(z'\)).
Why is the x-axis drawn slanting? Paper is flat, so we cannot really draw a line coming out of the page; a slanting line gives the eye a feeling of depth.

These axes are also labeled in accordance with the right-hand rule. The fingers of the right hand, pointing in the direction of the positive x-axis, curled images toward the positive y-axis, and the thumb will point in the direction of the positive z-axis.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "curled images toward the positive y-axis". The word "images" is a misprint; read: the fingers, pointing along the positive x-axis, are curled toward the positive y-axis, and the thumb then points along the positive z-axis.

blocks.alt: Simple line drawing of a right hand making a fist with the thumb pointing up. An arrow along the thumb is labelled +z. A curved arrow beside the curled fingers goes from +x to +y.
blocks.caption: Right hand rule: fingers curl from +x toward +y, the thumb gives +z (original line drawing)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Try it now: hold your right hand flat with the fingers along the x-axis, curl them toward the y-axis, and see where your thumb points. That is +z. A system that obeys this rule is called right-handed. If you swapped the x- and y-axes, the thumb would point down: that would be a left-handed system. We always use right-handed axes; this matters for the cross product in 14.3.

A point P in space has three coordinates, one along x-axis, the second along y-axis and the third along z-axis. If the distances along x-axis, y-axis and z-axis respectively are a, b and c, then the point P is written with a unique triple of real numbers as \(P(a, b, c)\) (see figure).

blocks.alt: Axes x, y and z from O. A point P(a, b, c) is shown with dashed lines: a vertical dashed line of length c drops from P to the xy-plane, and from its foot two dashed lines run parallel to the axes, one of length a (parallel to the x-axis) and one of length b (parallel to the y-axis).
blocks.caption: The point P(a, b, c): distances a, b, c along the x-, y- and z-axes (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to plot \(P(2, 3, 4)\): start at \(O\), move 2 units along the x-axis, then 3 units parallel to the y-axis, then 4 units up, parallel to the z-axis. The order of the numbers is always \(x\), then \(y\), then \(z\).
Special points: \((a, 0, 0)\) lies on the x-axis, \((0, b, 0)\) on the y-axis and \((0, 0, c)\) on the z-axis. A point with \(z = 0\), such as \((2, 3, 0)\), lies in the xy-plane (the floor); \(x = 0\) gives the yz-plane and \(y = 0\) the xz-plane. The three coordinate planes divide space into eight parts called octants.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Three mutually perpendicular axes meet at the origin \(O\).
Drawing convention: +x toward the reader, +y to the right, +z upwards.
Right-hand rule: fingers from +x curl to +y, thumb gives +z.
Every point in space has a unique ordered triple \((x, y, z)\); \(O = (0, 0, 0)\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Changing the order of the coordinates: \((2, 3, 4)\) and \((3, 2, 4)\) are different points.
Drawing the x-axis to the right as in a plane graph: in space +x comes toward the reader and +y goes to the right.
Using the left hand for the rule: the thumb then points the wrong way.
